That being said, it is also important to put virtual currency in perspective as a payment

Administrators of other major centralized virtual currencies report processing similar transaction

trillion in transactions, and Bank of America processed $244.4 trillion in wire transfers.
This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

such as cash transfer and distribution, and consists of 3 levels of due diligence:
Level 1: Confirm that the organisation’s Standard Operating Procedures have been
adhered to and check supporting documents for red flags.
Level 2: Enhanced due diligence to determine and confirm the bona fides of the entity
itself as well as its owners. This includes the application of open-source information
to build a profile of these entities and then determine their level of risk. This

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: Neutral — 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements may be implicated, but the facts do not establish that a covered financial institution detected the activity and had a statutory duty to file a SAR.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates the Secretary to require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides a safe harbor and confidentiality for such reports. Here, the fact pattern shows a Panama business (SYN_69fb5a14) conducting multiple large USD wires labeled “peel-chain hop,” with amounts (~$593k–$779k) that appear inconsistent with the declared expected monthly volume (~$597,008) and an enhanced risk rating—facts that could make transactions “suspicious” within the meaning of 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g). However, § 5318(g) applies as a reporting obligation only to a covered “financial institution” subject to the Secretary’s SAR regulations, and the facts do not identify any U.S.-regulated financial institution involved, whether the transactions were processed through such an institution, whether the institution detected the suspicious activity, or whether a SAR was required/triggered under implementing rules. Therefore, it cannot be determined from the provided facts alone whether § 5318(g) applies as a mandatory SAR-filing requirement in this scenario. Contiguous phrase: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious”.
